title: Elastic lease smoothing and tenant gating PRD
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a combined feature — Elastic Lease Smoothing (ELS) + Tenant Gating — to reduce oscillation in reserved GPU utilization, allow predictable short-term bursts, and contain noisy neighbors without hard preemption. Goal: keep customer-facing latency SLOs stable while improving overall cluster utilization and providing straightforward knobs for sales/ops trade-offs.

Problem statement (what keeps us up)
- Dedicated pools see frequent small bursts (startups testing, batch jobs, nightly churn) that cause repeated warmups and small autoscale actions, increasing cost and jitter.
- Current burst handling is all-or-nothing: either offer large burst capacity (wastes headroom) or strictly throttle (hurts UX).
- Tenants with spiky, short-lived traffic can degrade latency for steady-critical tenants in the same pool.
- Operators spend manual cycles moving customers or adjusting soft limits during seasonal peaks.

High-level idea
1) Elastic Lease Smoothing (ELS): convert a tenant's short-term spike budget into a temporally-smoothed lease that gradually decays rather than immediate reclaim. Instead of instant decommit when a tenant drops, ELS keeps a small warm shard of capacity (soft lease) for a predictive window based on recent burst patterns. This reduces ramp churn and cold-starts while allowing capacity to be reclaimed at a controlled pace.

2) Tenant Gating: a thin control plane layer that enforces isolation classes and dynamic gating policies (green/yellow/red). Gating is enforced per-route or per-API-key and can be configured by the tenant or admin with guardrails. Gate transitions are gradual (rate-limited) and observable via console.

Key user stories
- As a mid-market product team I want predictable latency during peak demos while retaining the ability to quickly absorb small traffic spikes without paying for fully reserved nodes.
- As an ops engineer I want to limit noisy tenants' effect on other customers with soft penalties, not sudden preemptions that break SLAs.
- As a sales rep I want a way to sell a low-cost reserved plan with burstability and a simple chargeback metric for burst minutes.

Design details
- Lease model: each tenant holds a primary lease (committed capacity, e.g., 8 slots) and an ELS buffer measured in lease-minutes (LM). LM is accrued by usage patterns (baseline + recent peaks) and consumed on bursts. Example: baseline commit 8 slots, ELS buffer 120 LM = ability to hold 4 extra slots for 30 minutes or 8 extra slots for 15 minutes.

- Smoothing behavior: when a tenant drops usage, ELS prevents immediate decommit of warmed workers. Decommit happens in phases: 1) fast-release fraction (50% of ephemeral slots released in 5m), 2) slow-release remainder decays across the ELS window. This is configurable per-customer.

- Gating classes:
  - Green: full QOS, allowed to use committed+ELS buffer, burst billing enabled.
  - Yellow: rate-limited to a configurable RPS or token-bucket; background tasks (like retrains) allowed at low priority.
  - Red: throttled heavily or forced into preemptible backplane (lower-tier latency).
Transitions between classes are based on signals: 1) observed tail latency impact on pool; 2) policy (contract tier, past incidents); 3) manual ops action. Gate transitions are rate-limited (no more than 2 class changes in 10m) to avoid churn.

- Burst pricing: propose measuring burst usage as "extra slot-minutes" per billing hour and charging at a premium. Provide a monthly burst allowance for enterprise tiers to avoid surprise bills.

- Admission and autoscale interplay: autoscaler reacts to aggregated pressure but ELS signals a damped demand curve (smoothed load) to avoid overprovisioning. When many tenants simultaneously spike, ELS will be allowed to promote ephemeral capacity up to a pool-level cap; beyond that, gating kicks in per the priority rules.

Operational controls and UX
- Console: per-tenant dashboard showing current lease, ELS buffer, gate state, predicted decay timeline, and estimated burst spend.
- Alerts: Ops SLO alert when pool-level ELS usage > 60% for > 10m or when any tenant enters Red more than 3 times in 24h.
- Runbook snippets:
  - If pool P95 latency rises above pool SLO and ELS usage > threshold: step1 reduce Yellow->Red candidates, step2 evict opportunistic workloads, step3 open incident and notify accounts impacted.
  - If a tenant is repeatedly going Red: contact CS for remediation; consider upgrading contract or moving to dedicated slice.

Implementation roadmap (MVP -> M2 -> M3)
- MVP (8 weeks):
  - Implement ELS lease-minutes accounting and smoothing playback in the scheduler.
  - Basic gating layer: three static classes + a rule engine to map tenant metadata to class.
  - Add console tiles showing ELS usage and gate state.
- M2 (12 weeks):
  - Autoscaler integration: use smoothed demand signal to reduce scale-up/scale-down flapping.
  - Billing hooks for slot-minute metering and burst allowance.
  - Policy UI for tenants to opt into burst purchase.
- M3 (ongoing):
  - Machine-learned ELS sizing (predictive buffers), churn-aware decay tuning, multi-pool coordination.
  - Fine-grained per-route gating, SLA-driven automated escalation, and migration assistant for persistent noisy tenants.

Success metrics (how we'll measure)
- Reduce autoscale actions per pool by 35% for pools with historically high small-burst churn.
- Lower P95 latency variance across tenants by 20% during simulated demo spikes.
- Average cluster utilization increase of 6% attributable to smoother lease retention.
- Fewer customer incidents related to cold-start latency during typical demo window (tracked via incident tags).

Open questions / risks
- Complexity vs. observability: will smoothing obscure true demand and delay necessary scale-ups? Mitigation: conservative tuning, visibility and guard rails that can force immediate scale if latency degrades.
- Sales/CS billing confusion: adding a new burst dimension may confuse contracts. Mitigation: default allowances and clear console breakdowns, early pilot with 3 customers.
- Abuse patterns: tenants could attempt to game ELS accrual. Mitigation: cap accrual rates and add anomaly flags.

Pilot plan
- Pick 3 willing customers: one mid-market with traffic spikes, one enterprise with strict latency needs, one startup with unpredictable demos. Run 6-week pilot: 2 weeks shadow-mode (compute ELS signals but don’t enforce), 4 weeks live with conservative caps and monthly review.

Rollout and docs
- Release notes: explain new billing unit (slot-minutes), default allowances, and controls in Console.
- Ops playbook: documented steps for mitigation and escalation, plus a migration guide for customers who need isolated slices.

Appendix: developer/ops TODOs
- [ ] Scheduler: add ELS state to tenant lease object and decay loop.
- [ ] Autoscaler: accept smoothedDemand API and ability to override smoothing for emergency scale.
- [ ] Billing: create extra-slot-minute meter and invoice line item.
- [ ] Console: charting for ELS buffer and gate state, policy editor.
- [ ] CS/Legal: update contract templates to include burst allowances and chargeback examples.

Notes to reviewers (informal)
- This is intentionally conservative: we want smoothing to reduce noise, not hide real demand.
- Looking for feedback on default ELS window (we proposed 15–60m ranges) and billing granularity (per-minute vs per-15m).
- Ops: is our alert threshold sensible? Ravi, can you run a quick sim on pool-nyc-1 traffic traces?

End.
